title: Iran War Bill Passes $47 Billion, India Becomes Europe's Shell Supplier, and Saab Pre-Positions a Canadian Gripen Line
subhead: The Pentagon's own estimate of the Iran war has climbed more than 25% since July, India's ammunition exports to Europe jumped over 1,600% in four years, and Saab lined up Canadian partners for a Gripen final assembly line while Ottawa's F-35 commitment stays under review.

sections.heading: The Iran war cost is now a budget problem, not a battlefield one
sections.body:
According to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters and reported by Defense News, the U.S. military has spent more than $47 billion on the war in Iran — over 25% above Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's July estimate of $37.5 billion. The figure has not been released publicly; the Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment.

The breakdown matters more than the total. Roughly $29 billion is projected to replace munitions expended in the campaign, and more than $6 billion to replace equipment and 'platform losses,' which explicitly includes aircraft and drones lost in combat. Defense News notes the estimate does not clearly account for the cost of repairing U.S. bases damaged by Iranian missile and drone strikes — suggesting the real number is higher.

The cost curve reflects the war's shape. Trump launched the campaign with Israel in February, betting on a short conflict and a strategy of opening with expensive precision missiles against Iranian air defenses before switching to cheap JDAMs. An April ceasefire let Iran dig out buried storage sites and bring some defenses, missiles and drones back online. Washington has since imposed a naval blockade and kept open the option of resuming heavy combat after the November 3 midterms, with officials telling Reuters the Pentagon is planning for exactly that.

On the Naval side, Defense One reported that Diego Garcia is effectively the only safe port for ships fighting Iran, but the atoll cannot perform the maintenance the warships need — port calls are degrading readiness.
sections.whyItMatters: Munitions replacement — nearly two-thirds of the bill — is the number that flows straight into defense industrial base contracts. A war the administration sold as short is now driving multi-year procurement demand, and it is doing so in the middle of an election campaign where energy prices are hurting the governing party.

sections.heading: India has quietly become a European ammunition supplier
sections.body:
India's defense exports to Europe have surged, driven by ammunition and artillery shells as European states refill stocks. Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said on Oct. 23 in New Delhi that EU 'ReArm Europe' demand plus India's expanding manufacturing base is driving the growth, citing a Bloomberg analysis based on Trade Data Monitor figures.

The scale of the shift: India exported at least $872 million of ammunition in the four years since Russia's invasion of Ukraine — a more than 1,600% increase over the preceding four-year period. Biggest buyers were Romania, Slovenia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Croatia and Poland. European destinations accounted for 40% of India's total arms and ammunition exports last financial year, per Samuel Rajiv of the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses. The basket is broad: artillery shells, small-caliber ammunition, mortars, propellants and explosives.

Two structural factors are pushing it further. A concluded India-EU free trade agreement, expected to take effect next year, will lower tariffs on Indian arms and ammunition. And New Delhi now wants industrial reciprocity — Singh said India wants joint ventures with European firms on Indian soil, with Indian companies seeking access to European government procurement in return.

Carnegie India's Dinakar Peri put the logic bluntly to Defense News: 'Russia is not an option for Europe, that is over. China has its own red flags in many ways in strategic areas and critical domains. So that leaves very few options available.'
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's ammunition squeeze has created a supplier that did not exist a decade ago. India is converting a commodity export (shells) into an industrial relationship (JV access, tariff relief, co-production) — the same playbook South Korea used to move from exporter to partner.

sections.heading: Saab pre-positions a Canadian Gripen line while Ottawa stalls on the F-35
sections.body:
Saab confirmed on Oct. 27 that it has formed alliances with Canadian aerospace firms to build, deliver and support the Gripen E in Canada if Prime Minister Mark Carney's government selects the aircraft. The team: CAE (Montreal) for pilot and technician training, mission systems engineering and sustainment; IMP (Halifax) for a new final assembly line plus electrical assembly and in-service support; Magellan Aerospace (Mississauga) for aerostructures, composite structures and structural assemblies.

The context is an unresolved fighter decision. Canada had committed to 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s, but the buy is under review after Trump threatened to economically cripple the country and mused about annexation. Canada has paid for 16 jets; two were delivered on Oct. 9 and Oct. 22, per Department of National Defence spokeswoman Andrée-Anne Poulin. Carney has not said when he will decide on the remaining 72. Saab is positioning the Gripen as either an alternative or a complement.

Saab already has a foothold: Carney announced May 27 that Canada will buy six GlobalEye AEW&C aircraft in a deal estimated at more than C$5 billion ($3.6 billion), with at least one-third of allied GlobalEye orders — projected at 40 aircraft over 15 years — to be built in Canada. On Sept. 25 Ottawa and Saab agreed a framework for the GlobalEye negotiations. Saab CEO Micael Johansson framed the Gripen teaming as delivering 'operational effect, national sovereignty and lasting industrial and technological benefits.'
sections.whyItMatters: Canada has decided its defense industrial base is a hedge against its closest ally's unpredictability. If Carney picks Gripen — even partially — the F-35's non-U.S. supply chain takes its first real hit, and Saab gains a North American assembly line.

sections.heading: Helsing prices drone interception under $100,000 a shot
sections.body:
Germany's Helsing unveiled Contra, a two-missile interceptor system with AI-driven engagement software, aimed at fast attack drones, at under $100,000 per shot. CEO Gundbert Scherf said it is in testing with market readiness expected in the second half of 2027; one contract has already been signed.

The engineering responds directly to how Russian strike drones have changed. Geran drones, derived from the Iranian Shahed design, were initially slow propeller aircraft that Ukrainian defenders intercepted at roughly 90%. Russia now fields thousands of jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 variants flying at 400-700 km/h, and nearly half are getting through, according to Scherf. Helsing's answer is a pair: AD-1 'Inferno', jet-engine powered, 700 km/h, 20 km range, for the bulk of threats; and AD-2 'Ambush', solid rocket motor at nearly 3,000 km/h, for last-ditch shots at leakers.

The commercially significant detail is the seeker. Helsing executives said the active radar seekers are built from widely available hardware, freeing buyers from Chinese-tinged supply chains and U.S. export controls. Defense News notes the launch comes as European governments fear U.S. systems like Patriot will become harder for allies to obtain after the Iran war.
sections.whyItMatters: The economics of drone defense have been the binding constraint — firing multimillion-dollar interceptors at cheap drones is a losing exchange. A sub-$100k Western interceptor with export-control-free components is the first credible European bid to break that equation, and it lands exactly when Patriot availability is tightening.

sections.heading: Poland wins the PAC-3 maintenance hub — but not yet the production line
sections.body:
The U.S. selected Poland to host a new European maintenance facility for Lockheed Martin PAC-3 Patriot interceptors, per U.S. and Polish officials. Supply chain integration for the hub will be led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden. Pentagon acquisition chief Michael Duffey said the move puts 'partnership into action' and called it a message that the alliance is 'ready to back our words with action.'

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk noted Warsaw had competed hard: 'We were contending against several ambitious competitors.' Poland signed a roughly $4.75 billion deal in March 2018 for two Configuration 3+ Patriot batteries, launched a second-phase request in May 2022 for six more, and in December 2025 announced the first two batteries reached full operational readiness.

The distinction that matters: this is sustainment, not manufacturing. European allies — Germany, Poland and Ukraine among them — are still lobbying Washington to permit local production of PAC-3 MSE interceptors to close supply shortfalls. Lockheed has said it is eyeing fresh interceptor production options for Ukraine and Europe.
sections.whyItMatters: Turnaround time on interceptor maintenance is a real combat variable at current expenditure rates. But a repair hub is the consolation prize — the production license, which is where the industrial value sits, remains un granted and is now the live negotiation.

sections.heading: C4ADS: Russian defense firms are moving production inside China
sections.body:
A new report from the Washington-based Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS), covered by VOA, finds Russian defense-linked companies beginning to embed production inside China, acquire Chinese intellectual property and use Chinese equipment to sustain manufacturing at home. Analyst Allen Maggard described the shift: 'It's not just China sending dual-use technology to Russia. It's Beijing tolerating Russian defense industry contractors setting up production inside China.'

Specific cases: Element, a sanctioned Russian microelectronics holding, reported assembling chipsets in China and incorporated at least four Chinese subsidiaries in 2025; in April 2026 it acquired power-electronics IP from Shijiazhuang Tonhe Electronics. On Sept. 30, Russian outlet CNews reported an Element-controlled company had delivered more than 100 pieces of semiconductor-production equipment into Russia and opened a Chinese subsidiary for logistics and quality control. VOA notes neither source establishes that Element produces military-grade chips in China or that the equipment goes to military customers. China supplied more than 90% of Russia's imports of high-priority dual-use goods in 2023, per C4ADS.

The asymmetry is the point: Moscow gets an immediate industrial lifeline. Beijing gets designs, testing capacity and expertise — consistent with SIPRI data cited in the report showing China's reliance on imported weapons fell 72% between 2016-2020 and 2021-2025. C4ADS also traced 12 shipments worth over $80 million from the Rubin submarine-design bureau to Chinese recipients linked to military procurement and state shipbuilding between 2015 and 2023.

Separately, SCMP reported on Oct. 28 that U.S. intelligence warns China is expanding its space toolkit with a spaceplane and directed-energy weapons, with a possible orbital weapons deployment by the end of the decade, and that PLA officers held talks in France and Germany despite trade tensions.
sections.whyItMatters: The dependency is running the other way from the conventional story. Russia is not buying Chinese weapons — it is renting Chinese industrial capacity and paying in knowledge. That is a worse long-term position for Moscow and a materially better one for Beijing's submarine and electronics programs.

bottomLine: Today's news is about money moving, not shots fired. The Pentagon's Iran war estimate has jumped from $37.5 billion in July to over $47 billion, with roughly $29 billion of that earmarked to replace munitions — a number that now underwrites a generation of missile and interceptor contracts. Europe's rearmament is simultaneously pulling in new suppliers: India's ammunition exports to Europe are up more than 1,600% in four years and are being converted into joint ventures and tariff relief. In the platform market, Saab has assembled a Canadian industry team for a Gripen final assembly line while Carney's government leaves 72 F-35s undecided, and Poland has won a PAC-3 repair hub but not the production license. On the low end, Helsing is trying to make drone intercepts cost less than the drones. Watch two things: whether Washington grants European PAC-3 MSE production rights, and whether Carney splits the Canadian fighter buy.
sources: Defense News, Reuters (via Defense News), Defense One, Bloomberg (via Defense News), Trade Data Monitor (via Bloomberg/Defense News), Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses, Carnegie India, VOA News, C4ADS, SIPRI, CNews (via VOA), South China Morning Post, Saab, Department of National Defence Canada, Helsing, U.S. Air Force, Pentagon
